_about: Buying costs, yearly taxes and the rule for foreigners, country by country (the data behind /costs)
note: General information, not legal or tax advice. Each country carries its sources and the date it was checked.

bali.can_foreigners_buy: No freehold (Hak Milik) for foreigners: leasehold, Hak Pakai (right-to-use, 30 yrs + renewals), or HGB title via a PT PMA foreign-owned company.
bali.purchase_costs_breakdown: BPHTB transfer tax 5% + notary 1-2.5% + legal 0.5-1.5% (GPG: 6.5-9%); new developer units add 11% PPN/VAT (stack ~17-18% without the 2026 PPN-DTP incentive, ~6-9% with it). Plain leasehold deals mostly notary/legal.
bali.annual_property_tax: PBB land & building tax, up to ~0.5% of assessed NJOP-based value (low hundreds USD on a $300k villa).
bali.rental_income_tax: Non-residents: 20% withholding on gross rent (10% possible under a tax treaty); PT PMA companies 22% corporate tax.

lombok.can_foreigners_buy: Same Indonesian rules as Bali: no freehold; leasehold, Hak Pakai, or HGB via a PT PMA.
lombok.purchase_costs_breakdown: BPHTB 5% + notary 1-2.5% + legal 0.5-1.5%; +11% PPN/VAT on new developer units unless the 2026 VAT incentive applies.
lombok.annual_property_tax: PBB, up to ~0.5% of assessed (NJOP-based) value.
lombok.rental_income_tax: Non-residents: 20% withholding on gross rent (10% possible under a treaty); PT PMA 22% corporate tax.

albania.can_foreigners_buy: Yes, apartments and houses freely; agricultural land is excluded. Title risk from communist-era confiscations.
albania.purchase_costs_breakdown: Notary 0.23-0.35% + lawyer 0.1-0.5% + agent 1-2%; transfer tax (0.5-3%) is paid by the seller (GPG, 2021).
albania.annual_property_tax: Local property tax ~0.05% of cadastral value (about EUR 75/yr on EUR 150k).
albania.rental_income_tax: Flat 15% on rental income, including short-term, declared via the DIVA platform.

mexico.can_foreigners_buy: Yes, but in the Restricted Zone (within 50 km of the coast or 100 km of borders, which covers Tulum and Playa del Carmen) only through a fideicomiso bank trust or a Mexican company; direct ownership elsewhere.
mexico.purchase_costs_breakdown: Acquisition tax 2-5% + notary 0.5-1% + legal 1-1.5% (GPG 3.5-7.5%), plus 0.5-1.5% for fideicomiso/permit setup; TheLatinvestor budgets 5-8%.
mexico.annual_property_tax: Municipal predial, set locally on cadastral value; usually small, often less than HOA fees.
mexico.rental_income_tax: Non-residents: 25% ISR withholding on gross rent; plus 16% IVA on short-term stays (Airbnb remits on its bookings).

spain.can_foreigners_buy: Yes, no restrictions at present; the government has proposed a 100% tax on (or ban for) non-EU non-resident buyers, not enacted.
spain.purchase_costs_breakdown: New build: 10% IVA + 0.5-1.5% AJD stamp duty + notary 0.5-1% + legal 1-2%; resale: ITP transfer tax 6-11% instead of IVA/AJD.
spain.annual_property_tax: IBI 0.4-1.1% of cadastral value (municipal), plus imputed income tax on unlet homes.
spain.rental_income_tax: Non-residents: EU/EEA 19% on net income; non-EU 24% on gross with no deductions.

montenegro.can_foreigners_buy: Yes, houses and apartments freely; land requires a local company.
montenegro.purchase_costs_breakdown: New build: 21% VAT is normally included in the developer price, buyer pays notary + ~1% legal; resale: 3% transfer tax (progressive on higher values) + notary + ~1% legal (GPG 4.01%).
montenegro.annual_property_tax: Municipal, ~0.25-1% of assessed value (higher rates possible for tourist properties).

georgia.can_foreigners_buy: Yes, residential and commercial property freely; agricultural land is reserved for citizens.
georgia.purchase_costs_breakdown: No transfer tax or stamp duty; registry fee 50-200 GEL, notary under 0.1%, legal 0.5-1%; agent 2-3% if buyer-paid.
georgia.annual_property_tax: Only for tax residents: 0.05-1% of value depending on household income; non-residents generally exempt.
georgia.rental_income_tax: 5% of gross rent on residential property (long- or short-term), residents and non-residents alike.

northern-cyprus.can_foreigners_buy: Yes, up to 3 properties (land cap ~1,338 m2), but each needs Council of Ministers Permission to Purchase (1-6 months); title-deed history risk.
northern-cyprus.purchase_costs_breakdown: Title deed transfer fee for foreigners 6-12% (sources disagree: 9% most cited, 12% in one 2026 guide) + 5% VAT on new builds (one source says 19%) + 0.5% stamp duty + legal GBP 1,000-2,500 + transformer fee GBP 1,500-3,000 on new builds.
northern-cyprus.annual_property_tax: Per m2, very low: about GBP 10-100/yr for a typical apartment or villa.

vietnam.can_foreigners_buy: Only buildings (mostly condos) on a 50-year renewable term, never land; caps of 30% of units per apartment building and 250 houses per ward.
vietnam.purchase_costs_breakdown: New developer apartment: 10% VAT usually already in the price + 0.5% registration fee + 2% maintenance fund + notary/admin; GPG lists 2.55-3.1% buyer costs.
vietnam.annual_property_tax: Non-agricultural land-use tax 0.03-0.15% of state land value; negligible for apartments.
vietnam.rental_income_tax: 10% of gross rent (5% VAT + 5% PIT) above the exemption threshold; threshold raised to VND 1 billion/yr from 1 Jan 2026 (older guides say VND 100 million).

italy.can_foreigners_buy: Yes for EU citizens; non-EU buyers need reciprocity (US, UK, Canada, Australia qualify).
italy.purchase_costs_breakdown: Registration tax 9% on a second home (resale), or VAT on new builds; notary 1-2% + legal ~1% + agent ~3% (GPG roundtrip 10-18%).
italy.annual_property_tax: IMU 0.4-1.06% on second homes (on cadastral value).
italy.rental_income_tax: Optional flat 'cedolare secca' on short lets: 21% for one property, 26% from the second.

portugal.can_foreigners_buy: Yes, same rights as Portuguese citizens (IMT increase for foreign second-home buyers announced Sept 2025).
portugal.purchase_costs_breakdown: IMT transfer tax 0-8% (progressive) + stamp duty 0.8% + notary/registry 0.9-1.2% + legal 1.25-2%.
portugal.annual_property_tax: IMI 0.3-0.45% of taxable value (urban), set by municipality.
portugal.rental_income_tax: Long-term: 25% flat for non-residents; short-term (AL) under the simplified regime only 35-50% of gross is taxable.

bulgaria.can_foreigners_buy: Yes, buildings and apartments, with rights similar to locals; per GPG, foreigners can't own land directly, so a Bulgarian company is the usual route.
bulgaria.purchase_costs_breakdown: Transfer tax 0.1-3% (municipal; Sofia 2.5%) + notary 0.1-1.5% + legal 0.5-1% + agent 2.5-3%.
bulgaria.annual_property_tax: 0.01-0.45% of the property's tax value plus a municipal garbage fee.
bulgaria.rental_income_tax: Non-residents: 10% final tax on gross rent, paid quarterly, no deductions.

denmark.can_foreigners_buy: Without Danish domicile or 5 years of past residence you need permission from the Department of Civil Affairs (Civilstyrelsen); EU/EEA citizens who live and are registered in Denmark can buy a permanent home without permission by signing a declaration to the Land Registration Court. Holiday homes (sommerhuse) need permission, which is only given to people with particularly strong ties to Denmark, such as many years of holidays there.
denmark.purchase_costs_breakdown: Registration fee on the deed (tinglysningsafgift) of DKK 1,850 plus 0.6% of the price, about 1% for a buyer's lawyer, and, if you borrow, a mortgage registration fee of DKK 1,825 plus 1.25% of the loan; the seller normally pays the agent.
denmark.annual_property_tax: Owners pay property value tax (ejendomsværdiskat) of 0.51% on 80% of the official valuation (1.4% above DKK 9.2 million) plus municipal land tax (grundskyld) at a rate set by each municipality, capped at 30 per mille of the land value.
denmark.rental_income_tax: A non-resident who rents out a Danish home is taxed in Denmark on the profit under the ordinary Danish rules; staying in Denmark more than 3 months at a time or 180 days a year, or working there, makes you fully tax liable.

sweden.can_foreigners_buy: Yes. There are no citizenship or residence rules for buying a home in Sweden, but you need a Swedish personal identity number or coordination number (samordningsnummer) to register ownership.
sweden.purchase_costs_breakdown: Stamp duty on the title (lagfart) of 1.5% of the price or tax value, whichever is higher, plus a SEK 825 fee; if you borrow and need new mortgage deeds (pantbrev), 2% of their amount plus a SEK 375 fee; optional legal advice; the seller normally pays the agent, and a cooperative flat (bostadsrätt) has no lagfart.
sweden.annual_property_tax: Houses pay a municipal property fee (kommunal fastighetsavgift) of SEK 10,425 in 2026, or 0.75% of the tax value if that is lower.
sweden.rental_income_tax: Non-resident individuals pay 30% tax on net rental income as capital income; for a private home you can first deduct SEK 40,000 per property and 20% of the rent (the 20% does not apply to a bostadsrätt).

norway.can_foreigners_buy: Yes. Anyone with the funds can buy property in Norway, and a built plot of up to 2 decares normally needs no concession (konsesjon) or self-declaration; owning property gives no right to live there.
norway.purchase_costs_breakdown: Document duty (dokumentavgift) of 2.5% of market value, a registration fee (tinglysingsgebyr) of NOK 545 for the deed and NOK 545 for any mortgage document; a flat in a housing cooperative (borettslag) has no document duty; the seller normally pays the agent.
norway.annual_property_tax: Some municipalities charge property tax (eiendomsskatt), at most 4 per mille of the value after a reduction of at least 30%, and some also give a basic deduction; many charge nothing.
norway.rental_income_tax: Rental profit is normally taxed at 22%, and the Tax Administration says its rental rules also apply to owners who are tax resident abroad.

germany.can_foreigners_buy: Yes. There are no restrictions on foreigners buying property in Germany, though non-EU buyers usually need a bigger down payment to get a loan.
germany.purchase_costs_breakdown: Real estate transfer tax (Grunderwerbsteuer) of 3.5% to 6.5% depending on the state (3.5% in Bavaria, 6.5% in Brandenburg, North Rhine-Westphalia, Saarland and Schleswig-Holstein), plus notary and land registry fees (Notar- und Grundbuchkosten) of about 1.5-2%; if the seller hired the agent, the buyer pays half the commission by law, which is extra.
germany.annual_property_tax: Owners pay property tax (Grundsteuer), calculated since 2025 as assessed value x a tax rate x a municipal multiplier (Hebesatz) that each municipality sets.
germany.rental_income_tax: Non-resident owners are taxed in Germany on net rental income at the normal progressive income tax rates, but without the basic tax-free allowance (Grundfreibetrag).

netherlands.can_foreigners_buy: Yes. There are no nationality or residence rules and no surcharge for foreign buyers. Some cities, such as The Hague, restrict renting out cheaper homes after purchase without a permit (opkoopbescherming).
netherlands.purchase_costs_breakdown: Transfer tax (overdrachtsbelasting) of 8% if you will not live in the home, such as a buy-to-let or holiday home, or 2% if it becomes your main home; a notary fee for the transfer deed of around EUR 500; Kadaster registration fees; and mortgage costs if you borrow; the seller pays its own agent.
netherlands.annual_property_tax: Owners pay municipal property tax (onroerendezaakbelasting, OZB) on the official WOZ value, at a rate each municipality sets, which in practice is a per mille figure; tenants of homes do not pay it.
netherlands.rental_income_tax: Non-residents declare Dutch property in box 3, where tax is 36% on a deemed return of 6% of the property's value in 2026, after a tax-free allowance of EUR 59,357 per person, regardless of actual rent.

france.can_foreigners_buy: Yes. Foreigners can buy property in France without major restrictions, and non-EU buyers do not need a permit, although the paperwork can take longer.
france.purchase_costs_breakdown: Transfer taxes (droits de mutation) of about 5.8%, or about 6.3% in departments that raised their rate for 2025 to March 2028; notary fee (émoluments) on a sliding scale from 3.87% down to 0.799% plus 20% VAT, about 1.3% on a €150,000 home; land security contribution (contribution de sécurité immobilière) 0.10%; disbursements (débours) of about €800 to €1,200; the agent fee is usually built into the advertised price (FAI) and paid by the seller, sometimes shared.
france.annual_property_tax: Owners pay an annual property tax (taxe foncière) set by the local authorities, and owners of a furnished second home also pay housing tax (taxe d'habitation), which some communes raise by a surcharge of 5% to 60%.
france.rental_income_tax: Non-residents pay French income tax on French rental income at a minimum rate of 20% (30% above about €27,500), plus social charges of 17.2%, or 7.5% for people covered by social security in another EU/EEA country or Switzerland.

poland.can_foreigners_buy: EU, EEA and Swiss citizens buy on the same terms as Poles. Other foreigners can buy an apartment without a permit, but usually need a permit from the Ministry of the Interior (MSWiA) to buy a house or land.
poland.purchase_costs_breakdown: Tax on civil law transactions (PCC) 2% of the value, paid by the buyer within 14 days of the deed; notary fee (taksa notarialna) capped at PLN 1,010 plus 0.4% of the value above PLN 60,000, plus 23% VAT; court fee of PLN 200 to enter ownership in the land register (plus PLN 100 for a new register); optional lawyer about 1%; the agent fee (about 2-3%) depends on the agreement.
poland.annual_property_tax: Owners pay a local property tax (podatek od nieruchomości) set by the commune, capped in 2026 at PLN 1.25 per m² of usable floor space for flats and houses.
poland.rental_income_tax: Private rental income is taxed as a flat lump sum (ryczałt) of 8.5% of revenue up to PLN 100,000 a year and 12.5% above that.

greece.can_foreigners_buy: Yes. Buyers from outside the EU and EFTA need a permit to buy in designated border areas (parts of northern Greece and eastern Aegean islands such as the Dodecanese and Rhodes). The government has announced a 15% transfer tax for non-EU buyers of homes from 1 January 2027, not yet final in September 2026.
greece.purchase_costs_breakdown: Transfer tax 3.09% of the price or the taxable value, whichever is higher; notary about 0.8-1% plus VAT; land registry fees about 0.5-0.7%; lawyer 1-2% plus VAT; if an agent is used, the buyer usually pays a commission of 1-3% plus VAT on top.
greece.annual_property_tax: Owners on 1 January pay the unified property tax (ENFIA), calculated per property from its location, size, age and official zone value, with an extra charge if total Greek property exceeds €500,000.
greece.rental_income_tax: Non-residents pay Greek tax on Greek rental income at 15% up to €12,000, 25% to €24,000, 35% to €36,000 and 45% above, after a flat 5% deduction for expenses.

switzerland.can_foreigners_buy: Under the Lex Koller law, EU/EFTA citizens living in Switzerland and holders of a C permit buy like Swiss citizens, and non-EU holders of a B permit can buy a home they live in. People living abroad need a cantonal permit and can usually only buy one holiday home in a tourist area, within national quotas; a proposed tightening was under consultation in 2026.
switzerland.purchase_costs_breakdown: Transfer tax (Handänderungssteuer, droits de mutation) 0% to about 3.3% depending on the canton; notary about 0.1-0.5%; land register fee, a small fixed amount or percentage; optional lawyer 1-2%; the agent fee (2-3%) is paid by the seller.
switzerland.annual_property_tax: More than half of the cantons charge an annual property tax (Liegenschaftssteuer), usually 0.01-0.3% of the assessed value, and owners also pay cantonal wealth tax on the property value minus the mortgage.
switzerland.rental_income_tax: Non-residents pay tax on net Swiss rental income at ordinary cantonal and communal rates plus federal direct tax, and some cantons set the rate using worldwide income.

cyprus.can_foreigners_buy: EU citizens buy without restrictions. Non-EU buyers need permission from the Council of Ministers, applied for through the District Officer, and are normally limited to one home or a plot of up to 4,014 m².
cyprus.purchase_costs_breakdown: Land Registry transfer fees of 3% up to €85,000, 5% to €170,000 and 8% above, halved for resales without VAT (1.5%, 2.5% and 4%); stamp duty abolished from 1 January 2026; lawyer about 1% plus VAT; small Land Registry charges.
cyprus.annual_property_tax: There is no annual national property tax (abolished in 2017); owners pay municipal fees of about €90 to €300 a year, plus sewerage and local authority charges.
cyprus.rental_income_tax: Non-residents pay income tax on Cyprus rental income at 20% to 35% after deducting 20% of the gross rent and loan interest, plus a 2.65% health contribution (GHS); the special defence contribution does not apply to them.

united-kingdom.can_foreigners_buy: Yes. There are no nationality restrictions on buying homes anywhere in the UK and no visa is needed, but buying does not give a right to live there.
united-kingdom.purchase_costs_breakdown: In England and Northern Ireland, Stamp Duty Land Tax (SDLT) is 0% up to £125,000 and 2% from £125,001 to £250,000, plus a 2% surcharge for non-UK residents and a further 5% if you already own a home anywhere, so a non-resident who owns another home pays 7% up to £125,000 and 9% to £250,000; solicitor (conveyancer) about 0.6-1% with a typical minimum of around £2,100 including VAT; Land Registry fee £20 to £230; searches extra; the seller pays the estate agent.
united-kingdom.annual_property_tax: Owners or occupiers pay council tax to the local council, and many councils in England charge second homes a premium of up to 100% from April 2025.
united-kingdom.rental_income_tax: Non-resident landlords pay UK income tax on rent at 20%, 40% or 45%, with 20% deducted at source by the agent or tenant unless HMRC approves gross payment, and the rates on property income are set to rise to 22%, 42% and 47% from April 2027.

united-states.can_foreigners_buy: Yes. There is no federal ban on foreigners buying homes, but about 30 states have added some limits, and Texas and Florida restrict buyers from certain countries such as China.
united-states.purchase_costs_breakdown: Closing costs vary by state and typically run 2-5% of the loan amount, covering title search and title insurance, recording fees, attorney fees, appraisal and lender fees; since August 2024 the seller no longer has to pay the buyer's agent, so the buyer may pay it unless the seller agrees to; FIRPTA does not apply when you buy but does when a foreigner later sells, with the buyer generally withholding 15% of the sale price.
united-states.annual_property_tax: Property tax is set locally and in 2024 averaged about 1.22% of value across the largest city in each state, from 0.30% in Honolulu to 3.02% in Detroit.
united-states.rental_income_tax: By default a non-resident pays 30% of gross rent (or a lower treaty rate), withheld at source, or can elect to treat the rent as business income and pay graduated rates on net income by filing Form 1040-NR and giving Form W-8ECI to the withholding agent.

canada.can_foreigners_buy: Mostly not for now: a federal ban stops non-Canadians from buying homes in cities and larger towns until January 1, 2027, with exceptions such as work permit holders and spouses of citizens or permanent residents. The ban does not cover rural areas and small towns, and the government has said it does not plan simply to extend it, but a replacement is being studied.
canada.purchase_costs_breakdown: Buyers usually pay provincial land transfer tax on a sliding scale (Ontario: 0.5% up to $55,000 and 1% from $55,000 to $250,000), legal fees of about $500 to $1,500, title insurance of about $250 and an inspection of $300 to $1,000, while the seller usually pays the agents; foreign buyers also pay Ontario's 25% non-resident speculation tax anywhere in Ontario and British Columbia's 20% additional tax in Metro Vancouver and four other regions.
canada.annual_property_tax: Property tax is set by each city as a share of assessed value, from about 0.3% in Vancouver to 2.12% in Saint John in 2026.
canada.rental_income_tax: Non-residents have 25% of gross rent withheld, but they can file a Section 216 return to pay tax on net rent instead, and Form NR6 lets the agent withhold on net rent.

japan.can_foreigners_buy: Yes. Foreigners can buy freehold land and homes on the same terms as Japanese citizens, even on a tourist visa, though buying does not give a visa or residency.
japan.purchase_costs_breakdown: The buyer pays an agent fee capped at 3% plus ¥60,000 plus 10% consumption tax (with a special cap of up to ¥330,000 including tax for cheap vacant homes up to ¥8 million), registration tax of 1.5% on land (until March 2029) and 2% standard on the building, real estate acquisition tax of 3% of assessed value, stamp duty, and a judicial scrivener fee of about ¥100,000 to ¥200,000.
japan.annual_property_tax: Fixed asset tax is 1.4% of the government's assessed value, plus city planning tax of up to 0.3% in urban areas, and small residential plots get a lower tax base.
japan.rental_income_tax: Rent paid to a non-resident is subject to 20.42% withholding (except when an individual rents it as their own home), and the owner must file a tax return each year through a tax representative in Japan to settle the final tax.

dominican-republic.can_foreigners_buy: Yes. Foreigners have the same rights as Dominican citizens to buy land and homes, with no restrictions.
dominican-republic.purchase_costs_breakdown: The buyer pays a 3% transfer tax (0% for qualifying first purchases under CONFOTUR tourism incentives), legal fees of about 1-2% and notary fees of about 0.25-1%, plus registration costs, while the seller pays the 2-3% agent fee.
dominican-republic.annual_property_tax: The yearly IPI tax is 1% of the part of a person's total Dominican property value, as assessed by the tax office DGII, above RD$10,695,494 in 2026, so a single cheap home is often below the threshold.
dominican-republic.rental_income_tax: Rent paid abroad to a non-resident is generally subject to 27% withholding.

ireland.can_foreigners_buy: Yes. There are no restrictions on foreigners buying homes in Ireland, and owning a home does not give a right to live there.
ireland.purchase_costs_breakdown: Stamp duty of 1% of the price up to €1 million (2% from €1 million to €1.5 million and 6% above), solicitor's fees of about 1-1.5% plus 23% VAT, and registration fees of €425 to €800; the seller pays the estate agent, whose fee is usually built into the asking price.
ireland.annual_property_tax: Local Property Tax (LPT): from 2026 a home valued up to €240,000 pays a basic €95 a year and one valued €240,001 to €315,000 pays €235; each council can raise or lower the basic rate by up to 15%, and most raised it by 15% for 2026.

colombia.can_foreigners_buy: Yes. A home bought by a foreigner counts as foreign investment, which needs no prior authorization and is treated the same as investment by residents. When the money comes in through the foreign exchange market, the exchange declaration serves as its registration with the Banco de la República.
colombia.purchase_costs_breakdown: Notary fees of 3 per thousand of the price (2026), customarily split between buyer and seller; registry fees of 9.11 to 13.33 per thousand depending on the price, plus 2%, paid by whoever asks for the registration, usually the buyer; and the registration tax (impuesto de registro), whose rate each department sets.
colombia.annual_property_tax: Impuesto predial unificado: each municipality sets the rate between 5 and 16 per thousand of the cadastral value (avalúo catastral).

uruguay.can_foreigners_buy: Yes. There are no limits on the types of property foreign buyers can purchase in Uruguay, and they have the same property rights as citizens.
uruguay.purchase_costs_breakdown: Transfer tax (ITP) of 2% for the buyer and 2% for the seller, on the cadastral value (valor real) set by the Dirección Nacional de Catastro; notary fees of about 3%; and an agent's fee of about 3%.

czech-republic.can_foreigners_buy: Yes. Foreigners can buy homes and land in the Czech Republic on the same terms as Czechs: the limits on homes ended on 1 May 2009 and those on farmland and forest on 1 May 2011.
czech-republic.purchase_costs_breakdown: There is no real estate transfer tax: it was abolished for purchases registered in the land register from December 2019. The land register (katastr nemovitostí) charges an administrative fee of CZK 2,000 for each application to register the sale (návrh na vklad); the notary or lawyer who draws up the contract is paid on top.
czech-republic.annual_property_tax: Owners pay a yearly tax on land and buildings (daň z nemovitých věcí); from 2024 the rates rose to 1.8 times their old level on average, and each municipality can multiply the tax by a local coefficient between 0.5 and 5. The return is due by 31 January and the tax by 31 May.

slovenia.can_foreigners_buy: Yes for citizens of EU, EEA and OECD countries (such as the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada), who buy like Slovenians. Citizens of EU candidate countries (North Macedonia, Serbia, Montenegro, Albania, Ukraine, Moldova, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Georgia) first need a decision confirming reciprocity, and citizens of other countries, such as China and Russia, cannot buy, only inherit where reciprocity exists.
slovenia.purchase_costs_breakdown: Real estate transfer tax (davek na promet nepremičnin) of 2%, paid by the seller unless the sales contract says the buyer pays it.
slovenia.annual_property_tax: The direct user of the home, usually the owner, pays a yearly fee for the use of building land (nadomestilo za uporabo stavbnega zemljišča, NUSZ), set by each municipality's ordinance and assessed once a year by the tax administration (FURS); owners of holiday homes also pay property tax (davek od premoženja).
